WTI fell 3.2% to $85.72. Silver plunged 3.7% to $47.00, its lowest since late 2025, with the gold-silver ratio widening past 82. Platinum fell 2.7% to $1,450; palladium dropped 3.9% to $968, breaking decisively below $1,000. Bitcoin held near $64,880, down 0.7%, stabilising after the weekend's plunge to $62,112 but failing to reclaim $65,000 convincingly. The Fear and Greed Index remains at 10 — Extreme Fear. overview: Oil led Monday's broad commodity selloff, with Brent crude plunging 3.6% to $92.44 per barrel and WTI dropping 3.2% to $85.72 — their steepest single-session declines since October. The catalyst was a paradoxical mix of escalation and diplomatic hope. Iran's IRGC claimed six vessels had caught fire and sunk in the Strait of Hormuz since the weekend, with UKMTO confirming a fresh projectile strike on a vessel leaving the strait on Monday morning, while Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy warned shipowners against using the American-backed southern route. Yet markets focused on the possibility that the unprecedented Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit scheduled for Wednesday in Shenzhen — the first face-to-face meeting of all three leaders, confirmed for the sidelines of APEC — could produce a Hormuz ceasefire or broader deal. Trump arrived in China on Sunday, adding weight to the speculation. The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt alongside the George H.W. Bush and George Washington makes three carrier strike groups in the Persian Gulf simultaneously, the heaviest US naval concentration in the region since 2003. Gold futures settled at $3,852, down 0.9%, as the dollar remained firm near 103.5 and the 10-year Treasury yield held above 5.15%. Silver plunged 3.7% to $47.00, its weakest level since late 2025, with the gold-silver ratio widening past 82. Platinum fell 2.7% and palladium broke decisively below the $1,000 support level, settling at $968.

The crypto market steadied after the weekend carnage but showed no signs of recovery. Bitcoin held near $64,880, down 0.7%, after the sell-off that wiped approximately $230 billion from crypto market capitalisation between Thursday and Saturday. The Fear and Greed Index remains pinned at 10 — Extreme Fear — and Ethereum traded around $1,818. Wednesday's calendar is extraordinarily dense: Anthropic's IPO prices at $70–$78 per share (approximately $1 trillion valuation), orders six times oversubscribed, with trading under ticker ANT on Thursday; the Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit could address the November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline, now 10 days away; and the IRGC's escalating claims and three-carrier US presence raise the stakes for any Hormuz discussion. Grains diverged — corn firmed 3¼ cents to 448¾ cents on positioning ahead of APEC trade talks, while wheat fell 6¼ cents to 587 cents and soybeans eased to $12.27 as the stronger dollar continued to weigh on US export competitiveness. LME base metals were mixed, with nickel easing to $15,860, copper holding near $13,610 per tonne, tin at $46,700 and zinc near $3,700. Newcastle coal held near $146, supported by the ongoing LNG supply crisis and approaching winter demand. The broader risk environment remains volatile, with the trilateral summit creating both upside hope for de-escalation and downside risk if talks disappoint.

watchItems.title: Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday — first-ever three-way meeting of the leaders
watchItems.text: The leaders of the United States, China and Russia will hold their first-ever trilateral summit on Wednesday, November 19, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen. Beijing has called the meeting one of 'ground-breaking significance.' Trump arrived in China on Sunday. The agenda reportedly includes denuclearisation (the New START treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving no binding limits on nuclear arsenals), the Iran conflict and Hormuz crisis, and trade. For commodity markets, the critical question is whether the trilateral format produces a Hormuz ceasefire framework or any progress on the November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony export-control deadline. The oil selloff on Monday — Brent down 3.6% — showed that markets are already pricing some probability of a diplomatic breakthrough. If the summit disappoints, oil could snap back sharply higher, while critical minerals would face renewed supply disruption risk.

watchItems.title: Three US carrier strike groups now in the Persian Gulf as IRGC escalates attacks and rhetoric
watchItems.text: The USS Theodore Roosevelt entered the US Central Command area on Sunday, joining the George H.W. Bush and George Washington — making three carrier strike groups in the Persian Gulf simultaneously, the heaviest US naval concentration since the 2003 Iraq invasion. The deployment coincides with an escalation from Iran's IRGC, which claims six vessels have caught fire and sunk since the weekend, including two tankers it says struck sea mines. UKMTO confirmed a separate projectile strike on a vessel leaving the Strait of Hormuz on Monday morning. The IRGC Navy issued warnings to shipowners against using the American-backed southern route, calling it a 'minefield of fire.' Iran's embassy in South Africa posted photos of two US Navy officers with threats. On Sunday, Iranian drones targeted a US radar installation at Bahrain's Riffa airbase, with Bahrain saying all projectiles were intercepted. UN Secretary General Guterres called for an end to the 'neither peace nor war' situation.

watchItems.title: Anthropic IPO prices Wednesday at $70–$78 per share — trading Thursday under ANT at ~$1 trillion valuation
watchItems.text: Anthropic is set to price its IPO on Wednesday, November 18, with trading on the Nasdaq under ticker ANT beginning Thursday, November 19. The offering of 825 million Class A shares at $70–$78 per share implies a fully diluted valuation of up to approximately $1.4 trillion. Orders are approximately six times oversubscribed. A separate private placement sees seven chip-and-cloud suppliers — Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC Partners — buying $26 billion of non-voting Class N shares at the IPO price, bringing the total raise to approximately $90 billion. The listing coincides with the APEC summit's most intense day and the Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral. Analysts continue to cite the IPO as a factor draining liquidity from crypto and risk assets as institutional investors reallocate.

watchItems.title: November 27 gallium, germanium and antimony deadline now 10 days away — trilateral summit the last window
watchItems.text: The November 27 deadline — when China's one-year suspension of its US-specific export prohibition on gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard materials expires — is now 10 days away. Wednesday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen provides arguably the last major diplomatic window to address it. The broader Busan trade truce was extended to January 10, 2027, but the specific export-control suspensions have their own legal instruments. The November 10 deadline for China's broader October 2025 controls has already passed without a published extension. Ex-China gallium remains near $2,100 per kilogram versus approximately $460 domestically — a roughly 4.5x premium. If the bans resume, Western semiconductor, defence and advanced-materials industries face renewed supply disruption. China produces about 98% of global gallium and dominates germanium and antimony supply.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: Down ~5.6% over past week · 10Y yield 5.15% · dollar 103.5 · Warsh holds hawkish line · trilateral summit Wed
desk.sum: Gold futures settled at $3,852 per ounce on Monday, down 0.9%, extending the sell-off that began last week to approximately 5.6% cumulative losses. The decline came despite geopolitical escalation in the Persian Gulf, as the dollar remained firm near 103.5 and the 10-year Treasury yield held above 5.15%. Markets are increasingly focused on Wednesday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen and its implications for Hormuz de-escalation and trade policy. CME FedWatch continues to price approximately 88% odds of a 25-basis-point hike at the December 8–9 FOMC. Central bank buying at approximately 675 tonnes year to date provides structural support but is insufficient to offset the yield and dollar headwinds.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: Lowest since late 2025 · gold-silver ratio past 82 · down ~20% from Oct peak · $50 support broken
desk.sum: Silver plunged 3.7% to $47.00 per ounce on Monday — its weakest level since late 2025 — as the gold-silver ratio widened past 82. Silver continues to underperform the broader precious metals complex, hit by both the rising-yield precious-metal headwind and softening industrial demand sentiment. The break below $48 opens the next support zone around $45.50–$46.90. With the 10-year above 5.15%, the dollar firm, the Nasdaq in a technical correction and three US carriers now in the Gulf, the macro environment remains hostile for silver's dual precious-industrial profile.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $85.72 · steepest daily drop since Oct · IRGC claims 6 ships sunk · 3 US carriers in Gulf · trilateral summit pricing in breakthrough
desk.sum: Brent crude plunged 3.6% to $92.44 per barrel on Monday — the steepest single-session decline since October — with WTI falling 3.2% to $85.72. The sell-off was driven by markets pricing a potential diplomatic breakthrough at Wednesday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen, combined with recovering Middle Eastern exports and IEA supply surplus forecasts. This came despite Iran's IRGC claiming six vessels had caught fire or sunk since the weekend and UKMTO confirming a fresh projectile strike on Monday. Three US carrier strike groups are now in the Persian Gulf — the heaviest concentration since 2003. The paradox of escalation producing lower prices reflects market conviction that the trilateral summit may produce a Hormuz ceasefire framework.

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME ~$13,610/t · LME stocks ~329,000t · dollar pressure persistent · AI data-centre demand structural
desk.sum: Copper held near $6.17 per pound (approximately $13,610 per tonne LME cash settlement), easing modestly on Monday. LME inventories have risen to approximately 329,000 tonnes, continuing to ease the supply tightness narrative. The dollar at 103.5 continues to make dollar-denominated commodities expensive for non-US buyers. Wednesday's trilateral summit adds uncertainty around trade and tariff policy. Physical supply in China remains relatively tight with elevated import premiums, but the macro headwind from yields above 5.15% and the strong dollar continues to dominate. AI data-centre and electrification demand remain structural long-term drivers.

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Up ~42% YTD · LNG JKM ~$32 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · winter demand approaching · 3 carriers in Gulf raises stakes
desk.sum: Newcastle coal held near $146 per tonne on Monday, flat on the day as the broader energy complex was dominated by the oil sell-off. Coal is up approximately 42% year to date as the Hormuz gas shock continues to revive thermal coal demand. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm of LNG supply offline. The escalation in Hormuz — with the IRGC claiming six vessels sunk and three US carriers now in the Gulf — raises the stakes for any ceasefire deal at Wednesday's trilateral summit. If a deal materialises, coal could face downside pressure; if talks fail, the energy supply tightness narrative strengthens further.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: Fell sharply on dollar strength · EV shift weighs on auto catalyst demand · hydrogen electrolysis provides floor
desk.sum: Platinum fell 2.7% to approximately $1,450 per ounce on Monday, extending the precious metals sell-off as the hawkish rate environment and stronger dollar weighed on the complex. Platinum has now lost approximately $50 from last week's levels. Higher borrowing costs, weaker vehicle production and the ongoing shift to EVs continue to pressure automotive catalyst demand — platinum's largest end market. South African mine supply remains constrained by ongoing power issues. The trilateral summit on Wednesday could shift sentiment if it produces a Hormuz de-escalation framework, which would ease energy costs for PGM-intensive hydrogen electrolysis projects.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Broke decisively below $1,000 · down ~31% YoY · EV transition headwind · weakest since 2018
desk.sum: Palladium plunged 3.9% to $968 per ounce on Monday, breaking decisively below the psychologically critical $1,000 support level. This is the weakest level since 2018 and the first sustained move below $1,000 in this cycle. The structural headwind from the EV transition — battery EVs require no catalytic converter — remains dominant. The break below $1,000 is technically significant and could trigger further stop-loss and momentum selling. With yields above 5.15%, the dollar firm and the macro environment hostile to precious metals, palladium faces a challenging outlook. Tight South African mine supply offers limited support.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: IRGC claims 6 ships sunk since weekend · 3 US carriers now in Gulf · projectile strike Mon · Iran drones hit Bahrain radar · 135+ total incidents
desk.sum: The Strait of Hormuz crisis escalated sharply over the weekend and into Monday. Iran's IRGC claimed six vessels had caught fire and sunk since the weekend, including two tankers it said struck sea mines. UKMTO confirmed a separate projectile strike on a vessel leaving the Strait on Monday morning. The IRGC Navy warned shipowners against using the American-backed southern route, calling it a 'minefield of fire.' On Sunday, Iranian drones targeted a US radar installation at Bahrain's Riffa airbase — Bahrain said all projectiles were intercepted and issued emergency alerts. The USS Theodore Roosevelt joined the George H.W. Bush and George Washington, making three carrier strike groups in the Persian Gulf simultaneously — the heaviest US naval concentration since 2003. Despite the escalation, Brent fell 3.6% as markets price a potential breakthrough at Wednesday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit. UN Secretary General Guterres called for an end to the 'neither peace nor war' situation.
desk.src: The National · gCaptain · UKMTO · Al Jazeera

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Firmed on positioning ahead of APEC · dollar headwind persists · WASDE tighter balance sheets supportive
desk.sum: December corn settled at 448¾ cents per bushel on Monday, up 3¼ cents, outperforming the grain complex as traders positioned ahead of APEC trade talks. The rebound came despite continued dollar strength near 103.5. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the November WASDE report continues to provide structural support. Wednesday's Trump–Xi bilateral (and trilateral with Putin) could affect trade policy, including the Busan truce soybean commitments. South American planting continues under generally favourable conditions.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Gave back Friday's gains · dollar pressure · SovEcon Russia export cut still supportive · APEC trade talks key
desk.sum: December wheat settled at 587 cents per bushel on Monday, down 6¼ cents, giving back a portion of Friday's rebound. The dollar at a 19-month high continues to weigh on US export competitiveness. SovEcon's Russian wheat export estimate of 36 million tonnes (below the USDA's 39 million tonne forecast) remains a medium-term bullish factor. Wednesday's APEC summit and the trilateral meeting could address the Abu Dhabi grain corridor, a potential bearish catalyst if stalled Black Sea shipments restart.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month $12.27 · eased on dollar strength · APEC trade talks could affect soybean commitments
desk.sum: January soybeans settled at $12.27 per bushel (1,226¾ cents) on Monday, down 4¾ cents, as the stronger dollar continued to weigh on US export competitiveness. South American supplies remain more competitive at current exchange rates, and Chinese buying interest is muted ahead of APEC. Wednesday's Trump–Xi bilateral could address the Busan truce soybean commitments, which require China to purchase at least 25 million tonnes per year through 2028. The USDA's tighter balance sheet from the WASDE report provides a structural floor.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,818 · $230B wiped Thu–Sat · Fear & Greed still 10 · Anthropic IPO Wed draining liquidity · no recovery above $65K
desk.sum: Bitcoin held near $64,880 on Monday, down 0.7%, stabilising after the weekend collapse that wiped approximately $230 billion from crypto market capitalisation between Thursday and Saturday. The cryptocurrency failed to reclaim $65,000 convincingly. The Fear and Greed Index remains pinned at 10 — Extreme Fear. Ethereum traded around $1,818. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows continued, with IBIT down 5.5% and FBTC down 5.6%. Anthropic's IPO pricing on Wednesday continues to drain institutional liquidity from risk assets. The 10-year yield above 5.15%, the dollar near 20-month highs and contracting stablecoin supply maintain a hostile backdrop. Key support levels are $60,000–$62,000 for Bitcoin and $1,800 for Ethereum.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM low $32s · TTF $28 · HH $3.00 · QatarEnergy FM through year-end · 3 carriers in Gulf raises stakes for LNG supply
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) trades near $32 per MMBtu, holding steady as winter demand approaches. TTF sits near $28 per MMBtu, while Henry Hub holds at $3.00. The IRGC's escalating attacks and three US carrier strike groups in the Gulf raise the stakes for LNG supply, with QatarEnergy's force majeure extending through at least end-December 2026, keeping approximately 5 bcm offline. The IEA projects 2026 global LNG output will fall about 3%. Wednesday's trilateral summit is pivotal — a Hormuz ceasefire framework could begin the process of restoring Qatari LNG flows, while failure would reinforce the supply crisis through winter.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · IRGC claims 6 ships sunk · 3 carriers in Gulf · trilateral summit Wed · 10 days to Nov 27 deadline
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. The IRGC's claim that six vessels have caught fire or sunk since the weekend, combined with the warning to avoid the American-backed southern route, further constrains Middle Eastern supply logistics. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). Wednesday's trilateral summit could be a turning point — a Hormuz ceasefire deal would begin to ease the sulfur supply disruption, while failure would extend the crisis. The November 27 export-control deadline is now 10 days away.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · APEC trade talks could affect fertiliser flows · Busan soybean commitment intact
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Wednesday's APEC summit and trilateral meeting could affect trade policy and fertiliser flows. The Busan trade truce extension to January 10 ensures China's soybean purchase commitments remain intact, supporting underlying grain demand. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: 10 days to Nov 27 deadline · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · trilateral summit Wed is last major window
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near 93,500 yuan per tonne. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. The critical catalyst is the November 27 deadline — now 10 days away — when the suspension of China's US-specific export prohibition on antimony expires. Wednesday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen provides the last major diplomatic window. If addressed, Western supply chains could stabilise; if the deadline passes without extension, overseas prices could spike further. The November 10 deadline for broader controls has already passed without a published extension.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: Up >130% since early 2025 · 10 days to Nov 27 deadline · China domestic Ga ~$460/kg · trilateral summit last window · Alcoa Wagerup FID but not producing
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium. Wednesday's Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen provides the last major diplomatic window before the November 27 deadline, now 10 days away. The unprecedented three-way format raises hopes for a broader deal that could include critical mineral supply. China produces about 98% of global gallium. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery in Western Australia has taken FID but is not yet producing. If the bans resume, Western semiconductor and defence industries face renewed supply disruption.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Firmer at $5.30 · upstream tightness in China and Europe · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, supported by persistent upstream tightness in both China and Europe. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but large-scale adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply. Wednesday's trilateral summit could affect vanadium indirectly if superhard materials restrictions are discussed alongside the November 27 deadline.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Retreated from $5,267 · ICE inventories at multi-year highs · supply optimism from West Africa tempering rally · El Niño risk persists
desk.sum: ICE cocoa eased toward $5,100 per tonne, retreating from Friday's $5,267 as supply optimism from West African crop reports tempered the recent rebound. ICE warehouse inventories remain elevated at multi-year highs, capping upside. Ivory Coast's Sodexam projection that 2026/27 output could drop 21–25% due to an 'exceptionally strong El Niño event' remains a medium-term bullish factor. Subdued chocolate demand and rising exchange stocks continue to weigh on near-term sentiment. The stronger dollar adds an additional headwind for dollar-denominated commodities.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Chinese refined cobalt futures rebounding to ¥260,000–270,000/t · Rotterdam $17–18/lb · sentiment improving but fundamentals weak
desk.sum: Cobalt is estimated near $35,000 per tonne, with Chinese refined cobalt futures rebounding to approximately 260,000–270,000 yuan per tonne and ex-works prices at 290,000 yuan per tonne — a significant recovery from early November's 200,000 yuan per tonne lows. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $17–18 per pound. The rebound appears driven by sentiment and capital inflows rather than a fundamental shift, with downstream buyers still purchasing on a need basis. The DRC maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027. The NMC-to-LFP battery chemistry shift continues to weigh on the structural demand outlook.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Near one-year low · structural oversupply persists · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028 · supply ramp-up continues
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate futures hover near ¥90,650 per tonne, close to a one-year low. Supply ramp-up continues to outpace demand growth, with new mine restarts adding capacity. Goldman Sachs projects a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Lithium's inability to rally despite broader commodity volatility underscores the structural oversupply challenge. The trilateral summit on Wednesday is not expected to have a direct lithium impact.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · oil sell-off could ease synthetic rubber costs
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight, with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Monday's sharp oil sell-off could ease synthetic rubber production costs, indirectly reducing natural rubber pricing support. Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles. The stronger dollar at a 19-month high remains a headwind.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot steady ~$91 · long-term contracts near $99/lb · IAEA: 78 reactors under construction · AI data-centre demand structural
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds at approximately $91 per pound U₃O₈, with long-term contract prices continuing to climb near record US levels of $99 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. The IAEA counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide and has raised its outlook for global nuclear capacity. Kazatomprom's TQZ sulphuric acid plant delays continue to limit leaching capacity. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver, with Meta, Amazon and Microsoft having signed nuclear power agreements. Wednesday's trilateral summit could affect uranium if nuclear arms control is discussed, though direct market impact is expected to be limited.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: Ex-China NdPr $109–121/kg FOB · CIF Rotterdam $100–120/kg · Nov 10 broader controls deadline passed · Nov 27 deadline ahead
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide trades near $72 per kilogram domestically in China, while ex-China prices sit at $109–121 per kilogram FOB, down $3 per kilogram. CIF Rotterdam ranges $100–120 per kilogram. Heavy rare earths remain tighter, with ex-China dysprosium oxide at $3,300–4,200 per kilogram. The November 10 deadline for broader controls has passed without a published extension. The November 27 US-specific deadline for gallium, germanium and antimony adds further uncertainty. Wednesday's trilateral summit provides a diplomatic window for critical mineral discussions.
desk.src: SMM · Rare Earth Exchanges · Benchmark Minerals

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners continue holding a firm pricing stance, with Comilog (Gabonese lumps) at $4.50 per mtu and Consolidated Minerals (Australian 46% lumps) at $4.80 per mtu. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The forward cost picture provides support, but soft downstream consumption limits gains.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: Eased modestly · dollar pressure · Indonesia RKAB quota tightening provides some support · surplus persists
desk.sum: LME nickel eased to $15,860 per tonne on Monday, down 0.3%, a relatively modest decline compared to the broader commodity sell-off. The dollar at 103.5 continues to weigh on the market. Indonesia's potential tightening of RKAB mining quotas provides a modest floor, but the global nickel surplus persists as Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions continue. Wednesday's trilateral summit and APEC trade talks add uncertainty. The macro environment remains hostile with yields above 5.15% and the hawkish rate outlook capping industrial metal sentiment.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: Eased from $48,295 cash · LME backwardation still wide · cancelled warrants elevated · Myanmar ban constraining supply
desk.sum: LME tin eased to approximately $46,700 per tonne, retreating from last week's $48,295 cash settlement as the broader base metals complex came under pressure. Structural supply constraints persist from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. The LME backwardation remains wide, signalling tight near-term supply. Cancelled warrants are elevated, suggesting further inventory drawdowns ahead. Tin continues to outperform the base metals complex on its significantly tighter fundamental supply position.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: TCs deeply negative · LME stocks declining · smelter curtailments continue · up ~23% YoY despite recent weakness
desk.sum: LME zinc held near $3,700 per tonne on Monday, essentially flat. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments. LME inventories have been declining, continuing the drawdown trend. The structural supply deficit that has driven zinc higher through 2026 remains intact, but the combination of yields above 5.15%, the dollar surge and soft downstream consumption caps near-term upside. Zinc is up approximately 23% year-over-year despite recent weakness. Wednesday's APEC outcomes could shift sentiment for base metals broadly.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,725 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · 10 days to Nov 27 deadline · trilateral summit last window
desk.sum: European tungsten APT trades at $2,725 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu. Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. The November 27 deadline for the US-specific ban is now 10 days away. Wednesday's trilateral summit provides the last major diplomatic window. The unprecedented Trump–Xi–Putin format raises hopes for a broader deal that could include tungsten alongside gallium, germanium and antimony. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · IRGC escalation raises stakes · 3 carriers in Gulf
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. The IRGC's escalation — claiming six vessels sunk since the weekend and warning shipowners against the southern route — further complicates the already dire supply picture. Three US carrier strike groups now in the Gulf represents the heaviest military concentration since 2003. QatarEnergy's Ras Laffan facility repairs remain estimated at 3–5 years. Wednesday's trilateral summit could be pivotal for helium if it produces a Hormuz ceasefire framework — Qatar and the US together supply about 81% of global helium, and any path to restoring Ras Laffan operations would need Hormuz de-escalation. Russia's export controls extend through 2027.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · grain mix of corn strength and wheat weakness
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Monday's grain divergence — corn firming while wheat and soybeans eased — produced a mixed near-term fertiliser demand signal. Wednesday's APEC summit could affect trade flows.
